title: Sierra Club v. Morton
summary: Aesthetic and recreational injuries can support standing, but the Sierra Club’s general environmental commitment did not substitute for allegations that it or its members used and would be harmed by development of Mineral King.
notes: Stewart wrote for a 4-3 Court affirming the Ninth Circuit (Powell and Rehnquist took no part); Douglas, Brennan and Blackmun dissented, Douglas famously proposing that environmental objects such as valleys and rivers should themselves have standing (drawing on Christopher Stone's 'Should Trees Have Standing?'); the developer was Walt Disney Enterprises, and the Club later amended its complaint to allege member use.

sections.Parties: The Sierra Club was the organizational plaintiff seeking to prevent federal approval of a proposed resort. The defendants were federal officials responsible for national forest and park administration. Walt Disney Enterprises was the selected developer whose Mineral King project required federal approvals.
sections.Material Facts: The Forest Service approved a plan for a$35 million resort with accommodations and infrastructure intended for 14,000 daily visitors. A proposed 20-mile access highway and power line would cross Sequoia National Park and required Interior Department approval. The Club alleged violations of statutes and regulations protecting parks, forests, game refuges, permit limits, and administrative procedures. It asserted its special conservation interest but did not allege that the organization or particular members used Mineral King in activities the project would impair.
sections.Procedural History: The Club filed in the Northern District of California in 1969 for declaratory and injunctive relief. After hearings, the district court granted a preliminary injunction. The Ninth Circuit reversed and identified the absence of allegations of personal injury beyond displeasure with the development. The Supreme Court’s assigned opinion concluded that the Club’s stated interest alone failed to establish standing. Amici described members’ camping trips, but those facts had not been presented in the pleadings or to the court of appeals, and the Club expressly declined to rely on individualized injury. The opinion left the Club free to seek amendment under Rule 15.
sections.Issue: Whether an environmental association may obtain APA review based on its longstanding special interest and expertise in conservation without alleging injury to its own activities or to identified members’ use of the affected area.
sections.Holding: The Club’s theory did not establish standing. Aesthetic and environmental harm could qualify as injury in fact, but the claimant had to be among those actually affected. An organization could represent injured members if it supplied that basis, which the Club had not done here.
sections.Reasoning: The Court recognized that changes to scenery, wildlife, and recreation could injure people who used the valley and park. The missing element was the connection between that harm and the claimant. Expertise and commitment alone would provide no workable boundary separating this organization from any citizen who preferred a different environmental outcome. Requiring personal injury placed the decision to seek review in the hands of people with a direct stake. The Court also rejected the Club’s asserted tactical dilemma: once standing exists, a litigant may invoke broader public interests in seeking equitable relief. Justice Douglas dissented in favor of permitting natural objects threatened with destruction to sue through appropriate spokespeople. His view sought to ensure representation for affected ecological resources; it did not become the majority’s standing rule.

topics.lrs-n-standing-injury: The opinion recognizes noneconomic harm but requires an affected claimant.
topics.lrs-n-standing-association: A membership organization can represent injured members if it establishes their injury.
topics.lrs-n-standing-apa702: The Club sued under APA § 702 as a party 'adversely affected or aggrieved,' and the Court held that provision requires injury in fact to the plaintiff itself.
